stories.headline: Replit's CEO says it has dropped Anthropic; a source says no
stories.standfirst: Replit chief Amjad Masad said onstage that "ChatGPT is better now" and the company no longer works with Anthropic, but a person familiar with the relationship told TechCrunch the partnership stands.
body: Amjad Masad, Replit's CEO and co-founder, said Replit no longer works with Anthropic, TechCrunch reported. Speaking onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday, he said the decision weighed "cost, partnership, and performance." He added: "I think ChatGPT is better now." TechCrunch is the only outlet that has the account so far.

On performance, Masad said Replit tests models on an internal benchmark and a public one, and that OpenAI's models, which he called "Sol and Astra," do better at building vibe-coded applications from scratch. He called OpenAI "a better partner for now." These are Masad's own claims about his company's tests, and Replit has not published the results.

The account is disputed. TechCrunch said a person familiar with the Anthropic and Replit relationship, who asked not to be named, rejected Masad's version and said the partnership remains in place. The outlet noted that Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, and that nothing had signalled Replit leaving Anthropic until Masad spoke.

TechCrunch pointed to recent evidence of continued use. A Replit blog post from late September listed Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 among models running in Replit Agent's production environment, and around then a Replit product employee posted on X about using Anthropic's Opus 5.5. TechCrunch said it had asked Replit for clarification and would update if it replied.

Masad also gave a few business figures at the event, according to TechCrunch. Enterprise made up about 2 percent of Replit's revenue last year and about 15 percent this year, and more than half of revenue is now business-to-business. He did not share annual recurring revenue. It is unclear whether Replit has switched its production models or is describing a change of preference.

stories.headline: Llmspeed shows how fast a local LLM runs on a GPU you lack
stories.standfirst: A free Show HN site streams text at the estimated speed of 29 devices, from an RTX 3090 to a 512 GB Mac Studio, though some figures are projections rather than benchmarks.
body: Llmspeed, a Show HN project that reached 46 points and 15 comments on Hacker News, simulates how fast a local language model would feel on hardware you may not own. Its tagline promises to let you feel local LLM speed before buying. Pick a device and a model, and the page streams text at the estimated speed, wait for the first token included, per its README.

The page lists about 29 devices and 15 models. Hardware includes the RTX 3090, RTX 4090 and RTX 5090, AMD's Ryzen AI Max+ 395 with 128 GB, a Mac Studio M3 Ultra with 512 GB, Nvidia's DGX Spark, a CPU-only Ryzen 9950X, and cloud cards such as the H100 and H200. Models include Qwen 3.6 and 3.8 27B, GPT-OSS 20B and 120B, Gemma 4 and DeepSeek V4 Flash.

The numbers come from two places, the README says. Measured figures are gathered from community benchmarks on r/LocalLLaMA, localscore.ai and llama.cpp discussions, and contributors can add more through pull requests. Setups with no benchmark get estimates labelled "Derived", interpolated from similar hardware, or "Projected", calculated from specifications.

The README explains the method: generation speed is treated as limited by memory bandwidth, with each token reading the active weights once, and only active parameters counted for mixture-of-experts models. Prompt processing is treated as limited by compute. Contributed benchmarks use llama.cpp's tg128 and pp512 results.

The caveats are real. The main page does not say which figures are measured and which are projected, and estimates are for a short prompt on a single device. The code is MIT-licensed, but the repository had only 18 stars when read on October 17, and nobody else has independently tested the predictions.

stories.headline: ChatGPT's Chrome extension can now read and drive your open tabs
stories.standfirst: OpenAI's updated ChatGPT extension for Chrome can compare products across tabs, fill in forms and group windows, and it is open to every ChatGPT plan, according to 9to5Google and The Decoder.
body: OpenAI has expanded the ChatGPT extension for Google Chrome so the assistant can see a user's open tabs and answer questions from them, 9to5Google reported on Friday. The update is in the Chrome Web Store. The Decoder, which cites OpenAI's own announcement on X, says it works with all ChatGPT plans, though neither outlet gives a rollout date.

Two modes do the work, according to The Decoder. Typing @chrome in a chat targets specific tabs, and chat mode can pull information from several at once. Work mode hands control of the tabs to ChatGPT, which OpenAI says can send messages, fill out forms, download files and group tabs. The full chat history appears in a sidebar beside the page being viewed.

OpenAI's own examples, as relayed by both outlets, are comparing products across tabs by size, material, shipping time and return rules, summarising articles in plain language, and matching price pages from different sellers. 9to5Google adds that OpenAI shows it filling out registration forms without submitting them and adding appointments to a calendar.

The Decoder says Work mode runs on OpenAI's Computer Use model and calls GPT-6 Astra the best on the market for complex, multi-step workflows. That is the outlet's account of OpenAI's positioning and has not been independently tested. 9to5Google likens the sidebar to Chrome's built-in Gemini integration, putting OpenAI beside Google's own assistant in Google's browser.

Several things are not in either report. Neither says how Work mode asks for confirmation before it acts, what happens to the content of open tabs, or what limits apply by plan. Those details may sit in OpenAI's documentation, which this report did not find, so anyone installing it should check what permissions it requests.

stories.headline: Gemini 4 Argon scores 97.5% on ARC-AGI-3, or 49.8% depending on setup
stories.standfirst: ARC Prize results show Google's Gemini 4 Argon at 97.5% on ARC-AGI-3 with a vendor harness, but 49.8% in the standard one.
body: Google DeepMind's Gemini 4 Argon scored 97.5 percent on ARC-AGI-3 using a Provider Adapter Harness, at a cost of $4,800, according to results from ARC Prize reported by The Decoder on 16 October. That makes Google the second lab past 95 percent, after OpenAI, whose GPT-6 Astra scored 99.9 percent.

The headline number depends on the test setup. The Provider Adapter Harness allows vendor-specific features such as retained reasoning and context compaction. In the Standard Harness, which allows only simple notes between rounds, Argon scored 49.8 percent at low reasoning, completing 42 of 55 games for $5,800, The Decoder reports.

Medium reasoning in the standard harness gave 46.3 percent. At high reasoning, Argon completed only 19 games, and ARC Prize published no score. The Decoder says API problems stopped Argon from finishing all 55 games, and that the reported figures include partial points from aborted runs.

On older tests, ARC Prize lists 91.3 percent on ARC-AGI-2 at $0.32 per task and 98.5 percent on ARC-AGI-1 at $0.16 per task. On the 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games, Argon needed 62 percent fewer actions than the human baseline, matching Astra, and equalled or beat the speedrun record in three.

Epoch AI's Capabilities Index puts Argon at 165, tied with Fable 5.1 and behind Opus 5.5 at 167 and GPT-6 Astra at 166, per The Decoder. Epoch's early estimates rank it eighth in math and sixth in software engineering. The outlet notes a similar harness dispute in July involving other labs' models.

stories.headline: Junior share of Anthropic technical hires fell from 27% to 9%
stories.standfirst: Anthropic's own economists report that junior staff were 9% of technical hires, down from 27%, as agents took on more work.
body: Anthropic published a report on 16 October describing how AI has changed employment inside the company. Its authors, who are Anthropic employees, say the junior share of technical hires fell from 27 percent to 9 percent, and the junior share of technical staff fell from 21 percent to 14 percent since early 2025.

The report says agent work hours passed human work hours in March 2026. By August, interactive agents worked six hours for every human hour in employee-directed sessions, although about 80 percent of interactive Claude session time is spent idle waiting for a person. Code commits per engineer are about five times their level six months earlier.

In a within-person comparison of 192 adopters and 74 non-adopters, code output rose after adoption, and proxies for quality such as lines later removed or reverted showed no difference. Non-technical coding-agent sessions rose from two a month in August 2025 to 90 in May 2026. The authors also report that account executives who adopted agents closed more deals.

The authors flag limits themselves. Anthropic is an AI developer with unusually deep adoption, so results may not generalise. People who adopt tools may differ from those who do not, the company was also growing fast, and the junior-hiring chart is descriptive only. More code or deals does not necessarily mean better outcomes.

The data comes from internal telemetry, headcount records, surveys, calendar data and 17 interviews, partly coded by Claude. Meta-work such as building agent tools rose from 10 percent to 22 percent of interactive sessions. No outside party has reviewed the data, and the paper has only the report itself to go on.

stories.headline: 91% of Anthropic staff expect a Nobel-level AI discovery by 2030
stories.standfirst: Anthropic's survey of 1,334 staff and 10,980 US adults finds 91% of staff, against 39% of adults, expect AI to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030.
body: The Anthropic Institute published a survey on 16 October comparing what Anthropic's employees and the American public expect from AI. It found 91 percent of staff and 39 percent of US adults expect AI to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030, according to the report.

On work, the gap is wider. More than half of staff expect AI to do at least 80 percent of their current work by 2030, against 5 percent of US workers. Average estimates were 75 percent for staff and 28 percent for other US workers. On suitable tasks, 59 percent of staff said AI cuts the time to a quarter or less, against 26 percent of adults who use AI at work.

The report also asked about the economy. Using a model-based method, it puts implied 2030 GDP growth at 17.1 percent for the median staff member and 5.4 percent for the median US adult. Workers who expect AI to do more of their work forecast higher unemployment, with those expecting 80 percent or more forecasting 12.2 percent, against a current 4.2 percent.

The samples differ. The US adults came from a Morning Consult opt-in online panel, fielded 11 to 23 August with 10,980 respondents and weighted to be nationally representative. The staff poll ran 9 to 12 August, was unweighted, and reflects personal views rather than company forecasts, the authors say.

A follow-up US sample in September, with 7,613 respondents, changed little, though the share expecting a Nobel-level discovery rose to 44 percent. The authors caution that the unemployment link is an association in forecasts and not a causal finding, and that visitors to their online scenario explorer are self-selected.

stories.headline: Jev reaches 35% of Vercel's paid teams in two weeks
stories.standfirst: Vercel says Jev, a small model from TypeSafe AI, reached 35% of its paid teams in two weeks, nearly double Sonnet 5.5's reach.
body: Vercel says Jev, a lightweight model from TypeSafe AI, is the fastest-adopted model it has seen in a first two weeks. TechCrunch reported the data on 16 October. Within two weeks of its limited release on 15 September, 35 percent of paid teams on Vercel's platform were using it.

That reach is nearly double the second most popular model, Sonnet 5.5, according to the figures TechCrunch cites. The numbers come from Vercel's AI gateway, a unified API service similar to OpenRouter, so they show use among Vercel customers only, and they may undercount labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic that also sell direct.

TechCrunch describes Jev as a model that picks from a set of predetermined outputs. Limiting the outputs makes it cheaper and faster than models such as Sonnet, which suits bulk classification. Vercel itself used Jev to replace GPT-6 Luna for classifying harmful commands, the outlet reports. OpenAI and Amazon have released competing models.

The same Vercel data shows open-source models account for more than 70 percent of tokens processed through the gateway and nearly 25 percent of total spend. Spending on frontier labs has grown tenfold, but its share of overall spend has shrunk, TechCrunch reports.

This is one outlet's account of Vercel's own figures. The paper has not seen the underlying data, and TechCrunch notes it offers little hard data beyond Vercel's platform. Nobody outside Vercel has verified the adoption claim or tested Jev's accuracy on the classification jobs it is being used for.

stories.headline: Apple bans hidden app features and names AI nudify apps in new rules
stories.standfirst: Apple's October 16 App Review update adds a rule against hidden, dormant or undocumented features, and lists nonconsensual intimate imagery as a content risk, after months of pressure over AI nudify apps.
body: Apple updated its App Review Guidelines on October 16, according to 9to5Mac, with changes aimed at AI nudification apps and at apps that behave differently after approval. The update adds a new Section 2.5.19, which says apps may not contain hidden, dormant or undocumented features, and specifically calls out code obfuscation. Apple says violations are grounds for removal and termination of a developer account.

Apple already barred hidden features under Section 2.3.1, 9to5Mac noted, but the new rule makes the requirement explicit. Apple also strengthened its language on apps that "misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities" afterwards, giving nudification as an example of what it means.

In Section 1.2, on user-generated content, Apple added "nonconsensual intimate imagery" to the risks it lists. Intellectual property infringement and anonymous bullying were already there. Developers who "fail to implement appropriate safeguards" may be treated as breaching the Developer Code of Conduct, as may those who do not fix violations after notice, according to 9to5Mac's quotes.

9to5Mac traced the pressure over the past year. The Tech Transparency Project found dozens of nudify apps in January. A later report said App Store search suggestions and ads steered users to them. Apple confirmed in April that it had privately warned xAI that Grok could be removed. San Francisco officials ordered eight apps pulled in July.

Section 5 also changes. Apps that facilitate human trafficking or child exploitation will be removed and blocked from alternative distribution, per 9to5Mac's reading. How strictly Apple will enforce the hidden-feature rule is not yet known. The reporting rests on Apple's published guidelines as summarised by 9to5Mac.
